t: LeetCode 1677 — Product's Worth Over Invoices: Per-Product Invoice Totals
o:
Two tables are involved: Product (product_id, name) and Invoice (invoice_id, product_id, rest, paid, canceled, refunded). For every product we need one row with its name and four totals - SUM(rest), SUM(paid), SUM(canceled), SUM(refunded) - aggregated across all of its invoices, ordered by name.

Walking the example: bacon owns four invoices whose rest values 1 + 1 + 0 + 1 sum to 3, and paid, canceled, refunded coincidentally also land on 3 each. Ham has two invoices giving rest 2 + 0 = 2, paid 0 + 4 = 4, canceled 5 + 0 = 5, refunded 0 + 3 = 3.

Because the task says "for all products", drive the query from Product and use a LEFT JOIN so a product without invoices would still appear, with COALESCE turning NULL aggregates into 0. product_id is unique in Product, so grouping by product_id is exact, and the final ORDER BY name satisfies the ordering requirement.
k: All four outputs are plain SUM aggregates over Invoice grouped by product - a single GROUP BY solves everything.
LEFT JOIN from Product to Invoice plus COALESCE(..., 0) keeps invoice-less products at zero instead of dropping them or showing NULL.
Names are guaranteed unique, but grouping by product_id (carrying name along) is the safer habit for strict SQL modes.

a.n: Approach 1: LEFT JOIN, GROUP BY, SUM
a.i: Join every product to its invoices, collapse the rows per product, and aggregate the four money columns. This is the idiomatic formulation: one pass over the joined data and exactly one output row per product.
s: LEFT JOIN Invoice i ON i.product_id = p.product_id.
Select p.name plus SUM of rest, paid, canceled, refunded, each wrapped in COALESCE.

c.python:
-- Database problem: submit this MySQL query.
SELECT p.name,
       COALESCE(SUM(i.rest), 0)     AS rest,
       COALESCE(SUM(i.paid), 0)     AS paid,
       COALESCE(SUM(i.canceled), 0) AS canceled,
       COALESCE(SUM(i.refunded), 0) AS refunded
FROM Product p
LEFT JOIN Invoice i ON i.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY p.product_id, p.name
ORDER BY p.name;

a.t: O(I + P log P) — one pass over I invoices; the ORDER BY sorts the P small product rows
a.sp: O(P) — one grouped row per product

a.i: Compute each of the four totals inline with its own subquery keyed to the current product row. It reads exactly like the four bullets of the task, making it a natural first draft, but it rescans Invoice up to four times per product, which is wasteful once tables grow.
s: For each product, select four scalar subqueries aggregating Invoice WHERE product_id matches.
Wrap each subquery in COALESCE so products without invoices report 0.

c.python:
-- Database problem: submit this MySQL query.
SELECT p.name,
       (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(rest), 0)     FROM Invoice WHERE product_id = p.product_id) AS rest,
       (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(paid), 0)     FROM Invoice WHERE product_id = p.product_id) AS paid,
       (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(canceled), 0) FROM Invoice WHERE product_id = p.product_id) AS canceled,
       (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(refunded), 0) FROM Invoice WHERE product_id = p.product_id) AS refunded
FROM Product p
ORDER BY p.name;

w:
Ship the GROUP BY version in interviews and production alike; mention the subquery draft only to show how English translates to SQL.
Watch-outs: an INNER JOIN silently drops products with no invoices; omitting ORDER BY product_name fails the spec even when the numbers are right; grouping by name alone is fragile even though names are unique here.
Likely follow-ups: filter to overdue products with HAVING SUM(rest) > 0, or extend the same pattern to monthly pivots with conditional aggregation.
